title: Which number can go with four when nobody says vada alone?
description: In the idli-vada game, one of the two numbers is four and nobody ever says vada alone. Testing each choice shows that every multiple of the larger number must be a multiple of the smaller, and Keeko's doubt, that only eight works, is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: no vada alone means every multiple of the larger number is also a multiple of the smaller. Watch for students who think the other number must be bigger than four, and so miss two.

source: Yesterday, we played this game with two numbers. We ended up
video_script.why: The child tests each choice by asking whether every multiple of the larger number is also a multiple of the smaller, and finds that two works as well as eight.
video_script.substitution: Test a pair by asking whether every multiple of the larger number is also a multiple of the smaller number.
video_script.anchor: the idli-vada game of the book, with one number four and nobody saying vada alone
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says only eight works, because the other number must be bigger than four. The other number may be smaller, and two works as well, so the doubt is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The other number could be two or eight

final_answer.spoken: the other number could be two or eight

maths_rules: idli goes with the smaller number, vada with the larger; nobody says vada alone when every multiple of the larger number is also a multiple of the smaller
ground demo: 3 and 6; multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, and each is a multiple of 3
other number 8: larger is 8; 8, 16, 24 are multiples of 4, so it works
other number 2: larger is 4; 4, 8, 12 are multiples of 2, so it works
other number 3: larger is 4; 4 is not a multiple of 3, so vada is said alone at 4
other number 5: larger is 5; 5 is not a multiple of 4, so vada is said alone at 5
other number 10: larger is 10; 10 is not a multiple of 4, so vada is said alone at 10
answer: 2 and 8; the book names only 8, but 2 works too
video_script.design: One idea: no vada alone means every multiple of the larger number is a multiple of the smaller. Assumes common multiples are known. Wrong idea: the other number must be bigger than four. The five choices stay on the board to the end.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the idli-vada game.
<bookmark mark='game'/>Two numbers were used in the game. The players said idli or idli-vada, but nobody said vada alone.
<bookmark mark='four'/>One of the numbers was four.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which of two, three, five, eight and ten could the other number be?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the pair 3 and 6; the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18 and each is also a multiple of 3

marks.pair: the pair 3 and 6 is written, idli beside 3 and vada beside 6
marks.six: the multiples 6, 12 and 18 are written under the 6
marks.all: each of the three numbers is joined by a line to the 3

narration: <bookmark mark='pair'/>Take the pair three and six, with idli for three and vada for six.
<bookmark mark='six'/>The multiples of six are six, twelve and eighteen.
<bookmark mark='all'/>Each one is a multiple of three too, so vada is never said alone.

beats.on_screen: Given: one number is 4; nobody says vada alone; choices 2, 3, 5, 8, 10

marks.given: the facts and the choices are written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, one number is four, and nobody says vada alone.

marks.find: the words To find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find which choices can be the other number.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: vada is said for multiples of the larger number; no vada alone means every multiple of the larger number is a multiple of the smaller

marks.rule: the rule for vada is written
marks.alone: the words vada alone appear with an arrow to such a number
marks.test: the five choices glow one by one

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step one, find the rule. Vada is said for multiples of the larger number.
<bookmark mark='alone'/>Vada comes alone if some multiple of the larger number is not a multiple of the smaller.
<bookmark mark='test'/>We must test each choice by this rule.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: test 8. The larger number is 8; 8, 16, 24 are multiples of 4. It works
narration: <bookmark mark='eight'/>Step two, test eight. The larger number is eight, and its multiples are eight, sixteen and twenty four.
<bookmark mark='works'/>Each one is a multiple of four, so vada is never alone.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: test 2. The larger number is 4; 4, 8, 12 are multiples of 2. It works
narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step three, test two. The larger number is four, and its multiples are four, eight and twelve.
<bookmark mark='works'/>Each one is a multiple of two as well.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: test 3, 5 and 10. For 3 the larger number is 4, not a multiple of 3. For 5 the larger is 5, not a multiple of 4. For 10 the larger is 10, not a multiple of 4. Vada is said alone
narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Step four, test three. The larger number is four, and four is not a multiple of three.
<bookmark mark='five'/>For five, the larger number is five, and five is not a multiple of four.
<bookmark mark='ten'/>For ten, the larger number is ten, and ten is not a multiple of four. Vada is said alone each time.

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The other number could be two or eight.

narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's doubt in a bubble, then struck through; the multiples 4, 8, 12 are shown, all multiples of 2

marks.doubt: the bubble appears with the word eight

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks only eight works, because the other number must be bigger than four.
<bookmark mark='two'/>But the other number may be smaller than four. Four, eight and twelve are all multiples of two.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Two works as well, so the doubt is struck.
